newsitem.title: CANADA: U.S. in deal for Canada to deport Saudi suspect.
newsitem.headline: U.S. in deal for Canada to deport Saudi suspect.

text.p: Agreement has been reached for Canada to deport to the United States a Saudi man implicated in the 1996 truck bombing that killed 19 U.S. airmen in Saudi Arabia, the suspect's lawyer said on Tuesday.

Lawyer Michael Wildes told Reuters the arrangement cleared the way for Hani Abdel-Rahim Hussein al-Sayegh to be sent to the United States from Canada shortly. Canadian authorities ruled last month he should be deported as a suspected terrorist but it was not clear whether he would go to the United States or Saudi Arabia.

Canadian court documents accused him of having been a driver in the Khobar Towers bombing last June and of being a member of the radical Saudi Hizbollah (Party of God). He maintains his innocence of involvement with the bombing.

Wildes said his client would have been executed if he had been returned to Saudi Arabia. "I expect him on U.S. soil shortly. A deal has been cut," the former federal prosecutor said in a telephone interview from his office in New York.
"I believe that the arrangement serves both the interests of protecting my client's safety and the U.S. government's interest in investigating the Khobar Towers bombing."

Wildes said he would appear with Sayegh in Federal Court in Washington in the next few days. Justice Department officials said this would be one or two days after Sayegh's arrival, now thought to be most likely on Wednesday.

He gave few details on the arrangement but a source in Canada familiar with the deal said it involved Sayegh passing a lie detector test that he was not involved in the Khobar Towers bombing in eastern Saudi Arabia last June.
"They will be able to investigate the Khobar Towers bombing and get some pretty serious intelligence information in that regard," Wildes said.

Sayegh, a quiet, clean-cut young man, arrived in Ottawa from the Middle East in August, traveling through Boston and thus providing legal grounds for deportation to the United States. He applied for asylum in Canada on the grounds that as a Shi'ite Muslim activist he was persecuted by the government of Saudi Arabia, whose rulers are Sunni Muslims.
"Of paramount importance to me is his physical welfare and that of his wife and two children that are still in Saudi Arabia," Wildes said.

"He clearly is a minority Shi'ite and has been outspoken on his pro-democracy beliefs. If only for those political beliefs he would be executed. Because of the sensitive nature of the intelligence that he has, he would most certainly meet with death if he returns to Saudi Arabia."
The Washington Post reported on Tuesday that Sayegh would plead guilty to an unrelated extremist attack that was never carried out, but Wildes said this was not true.
